prompt.context: Your firm has won an RFP to help a domestic airline carrier examine their in-flight connectivity (IFC) strategy. With 80% of US-based aircraft already outfitted with IFC technology and competitive pressures rising, offering WiFi service is becoming table-stakes. Your client has yet to enter the game, but they know it's something they need to consider to stay competitive.
prompt.question: What are some of the key things the client should think about when assessing their go-to-market strategy for IFC?

clarifying_info.q: What routes does the airline fly?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily domestic routes within the continental US, as well as select flights to Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
IFC includes only WiFi connectivity. In-flight entertainment (IFE) is delivered via an on-board server through a separate system, but the two can be integrated into one user experience.

clarifying_info.q: What is the airline's main objective?
clarifying_info.a: The airline's main objective is to stay competitive.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the airline's fleet and how many flights does it service?
clarifying_info.a: The airline has 90 planes and services approximately 30,000 flights per year.

clarifying_info.q: How is IFC typically installed and managed?
clarifying_info.a: IFC is typically installed and managed by an outside vendor, either through a branded service (e.g., GoGoAir) or a wholesale, white-label solution (e.g., Row44). Contracts are typically 10+ years long.

clarifying_info.q: Do different vendors use different technologies?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, different vendors use different technologies, which vary in quality.

clarifying_info.q: How does bandwidth work with multiple users?
clarifying_info.a: Total bandwidth is shared across passengers, so the more passengers buy a session, the slower the service. Some carriers intentionally charge high prices to limit usage and ensure better service.

exhibits.title: Competitive Benchmarking
exhibits.shows: A table comparing two competitor airlines across four dimensions of their IFC business models.

rows.competitor_1: Major domestic and international carrier with 65% fleet IFC coverage
rows.competitor_2: Domestic discount carrier with 90% fleet IFC coverage

exhibits.title: Air Fleet Statistics
exhibits.shows: A table showing fleet composition and operating statistics broken down by aircraft body type (wide body vs. narrow body).

framework: Pricing and pricing model (free, ad-supported, pay per data usage, pay per time, pay by speed tier, subscription service)
Market demand: take rate and market segments
Costs: upfront investment (capex) and ongoing operating costs
Vendor contract structure: revenue/business model, split of investment costs and OpEx, branding, contract length, technology
Product and user experience: built-in screens vs. BYO-screen, white-label vs. vendor-branding, speeds available, interoperability with IFE, add-on services
Technology: speed, bandwidth, latency, availability when flying over water
GTM: rollout timing, marketing, crew training, ad sales

questions.prompt: Review the competitive benchmarking data (Exhibit 1). What are your thoughts on the two competitor business models?
questions.guidance:
Candidate should compare pros and cons of each model and recognize these are not the only two possible models. Strong candidates will consider elements beyond those in the exhibit.

Competitor 1 (Vendor-branded, revenue share, $25/session set by vendor):
- Pros: less operational burden on airline, potential for customer experience continuity (e.g., allow subscriptions across airline carriers), limited costs for airline
- Cons: limited control over pricing (high price could drive low take rates and anger customers), brand fit considerations

Competitor 2 (Airline-branded, wholesale, free for customers):
- Pros: control over pricing, control over user experience, potential for better ROI, easier to integrate with airline's other products (e.g., IFE system)
- Cons: more operational burden on airline, higher costs

Other considerations: who pays for the initial investment, ongoing cost structure, potential to adopt more than one model across the fleet, technology limitations (vendors are not equal). Assume 1 session buys a passenger WiFi connectivity for the duration of the flight.

questions.prompt: The client has decided to partner with a white-label IFC vendor to outfit all 90 planes. The airline and vendor will share the initial investment, and then the airline will pay the vendor a per-session fee to cover operating expenses. What percentage of passengers need to purchase a session for the airline to break even in 2 years? (Use Exhibit 2; capex = $250K per plane with airline covering 40%; margin = $10 per session — provide only when asked)
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up a break-even equation: total investment divided by (total passengers x margin per session). Strong candidates will surface assumptions about seat occupancy and rollout timing, and will react to the result with a strategic implication.

math.setup:
Break-even take rate = Total Investment / (Total Passengers over 2 yrs x Margin per session)
Airline share of investment = $250K x 40% = $100K per plane
Total investment = (10 wide-body x $100K) + (80 narrow-body x $100K)
Total passengers = (wide-body seats x wide-body flights x 2 yrs) + (narrow-body seats x narrow-body flights x 2 yrs)
Solve: Total passengers x take rate x $10 = Total investment
steps: Wide-body passengers: 300 seats x 2,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 1.5M
Narrow-body passengers: 100 seats x 27,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 5.5M
math.answer: ~12.9% take rate required to break even in 2 years (assumptions: 100% seat occupancy, all aircraft outfitted simultaneously, ad revenues baked into margin figures, 1 session per flight per passenger)

questions.prompt: Market research tells us that take rates are only between 5% and 10% today for paid connectivity, so the client is concerned about hitting the break-even targets. What do you think are the key drivers of IFC take rate?
questions.guidance:
This is a correlation question (what variables correlate with higher take rates), not causation. Candidate should brainstorm broadly across multiple categories and hypothesize the direction of each variable's effect on take rate.
- Flight characteristics: flight length (longer = higher take rate), flight time (red-eye vs. daytime), availability of other entertainment systems
- Product characteristics: price (lower = higher take rate), speeds available, quality of service, number of connected devices allowed
- Passenger characteristics: age, gender, income level, cabin class (business vs. economy), travel purpose (business vs. leisure)
Interviewer should push candidate to hypothesize which direction each variable would need to swing to drive higher take rate.

brainstorming.prompt: What do you think are the key drivers of IFC take rate?

categories.name: Flight characteristics
ideas: Flight length (longer flights correlate with higher take rate)
Availability of other in-flight entertainment options

categories.name: Product characteristics
ideas: Price (lower price drives higher take rate)

categories.name: Passenger characteristics
ideas: Age (younger passengers more likely to purchase)
Cabin class (business travelers more likely to purchase)

recommendation: The airline should partner with a wholesale, white-label vendor to retain control over pricing and the user experience
Roll-out across aircraft should be gradual, with a potential pilot program to optimize pricing, user experience, etc.
Roll-out should prioritize newer planes that cover routes with high expected take rates
risks: Due to the large upfront investment, the contract is likely to be 10+ years long, making smart vendor selection very critical
Difficult to strike the right balance between maximizing revenue and maintaining a sufficiently low take rate to ensure higher speeds
Technology is still nascent, with potential for poor user experience
next_steps: Aircraft prioritization (route analysis to identify highest-take-rate opportunities)
Pilot launch to test pricing, UX, and operational processes
